title: Supported cohomology and canonical residue on a strictly henselian trait
statement:
Let $\ell$ be a prime, $\Lambda=\mathbf F_\ell$, and $T=\operatorname{Spec}R$ for a strictly henselian discrete valuation ring on which $\ell$ is invertible [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring]. Write $s,\eta$ for its closed and generic points, choose a geometric generic point $\bar\eta$, and let $p$ be the characteristic exponent of $\kappa(s)$ (equal to $1$ in characteristic zero) [def-weil-geometric-point], [def-weil-residue-field]. Put $H=\operatorname{Gal}(\kappa(\bar\eta)/\kappa(\eta))$, understood as the automorphism group of the separable closure inside the chosen algebraic closure, with its profinite topology. There is a canonical tame quotient $H\twoheadrightarrow G=\widehat{\mathbf Z}^{(p')}(1)$ with kernel $S$, whose finite continuous quotients have $p$-power order; for $p=1$, $S=1$. Here $G=\varprojlim_{(d,p)=1}\mu_d(\kappa(\bar\eta))$, with transition maps given by powers; the quotient sends an automorphism to its actions on compatible prime-to-$p$ roots of a uniformizer.

Let $A=\Lambda[[G]]=\varprojlim_U\Lambda[G/U]$, where $U$ ranges over open subgroups, and $I=\ker(A\xrightarrow{\epsilon}\Lambda)$, where $\epsilon$ sums coefficients. For every topological generator $\sigma$ of $G$, multiplication by $1-\sigma$ is an isomorphism of $A$-modules $A\xrightarrow{\sim}I$.

For a sheaf $M$ of $\Lambda$-modules on $T_{\mathrm{et}}$, let $M_s$ be its closed geometric stalk and $M_{\bar\eta}$ its geometric generic stalk with its continuous $H$-action. The specialization of stalks lands in $M_{\bar\eta}^S$. Define the complex
$$F(M)=\bigl[M_s\longrightarrow M_{\bar\eta}^S\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,M_{\bar\eta}^S)\bigr]$$
in degrees $0,1,2$, where the last differential sends $m$ to $(a\mapsto am)$. The additive functor $F$ is exact. For every bounded below complex $K$ of such sheaves, its total complex $F(K)$ represents $R\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,K)$ [def-pur-etale-derived-supported-sections], [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories], naturally in $K$; in particular $F$ preserves quasi-isomorphisms.

Averaging over the finite $p$-group quotients acting on each vector defines a canonical projector $\operatorname{av}_S:M_{\bar\eta}\to M_{\bar\eta}^S$. For a discrete $\Lambda$-module $N$, put $N(-1)=\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(\mu_\ell(\kappa(\bar\eta)),N)$. The identification $N(-1)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(G,N)$ uses the underlying additive group of $N$ with no equivariance condition on this Hom. Evaluation at $\sigma$, followed by the inverse of evaluation at $1-\sigma$ on $\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,M_{\bar\eta}^S)$, and preceded by $\operatorname{av}_S$, defines a natural cochain map
$$s_\sigma:M_{\bar\eta}(-1)\longrightarrow F(M)[2].$$
For any two topological generators these cochain maps have a unique homotopy natural in the sheaf $M$. Termwise application and totalization therefore give a morphism
$$\operatorname{sp}_T:K_{\bar\eta}\longrightarrow R\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,K)(1)[2]$$
in $D^+(\Lambda)$, independent of the generator and of the representing complex, natural in $K$. Here $(1)$ is tensor with $\mu_\ell(\kappa(\bar\eta))$, and $[2]$ is the cohomological shift.

source.place: Expose XVII, sections 1.2.1–1.2.3, Proposition 1.2.1.2, Proposition 1.2.2.1 and Lemma 1.2.3.2 (printed pp. 259–262; n=ell)

proof.text: Use [lem-per-trait-tame-algebra] for the exact sequence $1\to S\to H\to G\to1$, its canonical root-of-uniformizer formula, the pro-$p$ property, and a generator $\sigma$ of $G$. For $(d,p)=1$ put $B_d=\Lambda[G/\overline{\langle\sigma^d\rangle}]$. These finite cyclic quotients form the inverse system defining $A$. We now prove, rather than assume, the augmentation assertion left as an exercise in Proposition 1.2.1.2.

Write $z$ for the image of $\sigma$ in $B_d$. Coefficient comparison gives $\ker(1-z:B_d\to B_d)=\Lambda N_d$, where $N_d=1+z+\cdots+z^{d-1}$. If $x=\sum a_i z^i$ and $\sum a_i=0$, set $b_0=0$ and $b_i=\sum_{j=1}^i a_j$ for $1\le i<d$; then $(1-z)\sum b_i z^i=x$. Thus the image of $1-z$ is exactly the augmentation ideal. For a compatible augmentation-zero family $x_d$, define $b_d$ by projecting any solution of $(1-z)b=x_{\ell d}$ from $B_{\ell d}$ to $B_d$. This is independent of the solution because $N_{\ell d}$ projects to $\ell N_d=0$. For $d\mid e$, projecting a solution at $\ell e$ through $\ell d$ proves compatibility of the $b_d$. They give $b\in A$ with $(1-\sigma)b=x$. If $(1-\sigma)b=0$, the component $b_d$ is the image of a multiple of $N_{\ell d}$, hence zero. Consequently $1-\sigma:A\to I$ is bijective and $A$-linear.

source.place: Proposition 1.2.1.2 (printed p. 260), finite-cyclic coefficient proof of the exercise

proof.text: By [lem-per-trait-sheaf-gluing], write a sheaf as $(W,V,a)$ with $W=M_s$, $V=M_{\bar\eta}$ and $a(W)\subset V^H\subset V^S$. Both stalk functors are exact because kernels and cokernels of these triples are componentwise. For $v\in V$, choose an open normal subgroup $U\subset S$ fixing $v$ and put $\operatorname{av}_S(v)=|S/U|^{-1}\sum_{g\in S/U}gv$. This does not change on refining $U$: each summand is repeated $[U:U']$ times. Common refinements prove additivity and linearity. It is natural, fixes $V^S$ and has image in $V^S$. Since $S$ is normal, conjugating the finite sum shows $H$-equivariance. If an invariant vector is lifted through an equivariant surjection, averaging a lift gives an invariant lift. Thus $(-)^S$ is exact (also when $p=1$). Evaluation at $1-\sigma$ identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,V^S)$ with $V^S$, so it too is exact. The indicated differentials square to zero since $a(W)\subset V^H$. This proves exactness of the functor $F$ in every degree.

Suppose $M$ is injective. In the triple description, $V\mapsto(0,V,0)$ is an exact left adjoint to restriction $(W,V,a)\mapsto V$. Hence [lem-exc-rg-right-adjoint-preserves-injectives] shows that $V$ is injective in discrete $H$-modules. Inflation from discrete $G$-modules to discrete $H$-modules is exact; its right adjoint is $V\mapsto V^S$, because an $H$-map from an inflated module has image in $V^S$. The same cited adjoint theorem makes $N=V^S$ injective in discrete $G$-modules. This is precisely the restriction to $\eta$, followed by the direct image $\eta_{\mathrm{et}}\to BG$, used in the source; it needs no assertion that the compact modules $A$ or $I$ are discrete.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 1.2.2.1 (printed p. 260), injectivity via the generic-to-tame topos morphism

proof.text: For every $M=(W,V,a)$ the kernel of $V^S\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,V^S)$ is $V^H$: it consists of vectors killed by $1-\sigma$, hence fixed by dense powers of $\sigma$ and thus by $G$. In particular this kernel is $\Gamma(\eta,M|_\eta)$, not sections supported at $s$. By [lem-per-trait-sheaf-gluing] and the definition of supported sections [def-pur-etale-derived-supported-sections], $H^0(F(M))=\ker(W\to V^H)=\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,M)$. For injective $M$, any $v\in V^H$ defines a morphism $(0,\Lambda,0)\to M$ by $1\mapsto v$. Extend it along the monomorphism $(0,\Lambda,0)\hookrightarrow(\Lambda,\Lambda,\mathrm{id})$. The closed component of the extension supplies $w\in W$ with $a(w)=v$. Therefore $H^1(F(M))=0$.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 1.2.2.1 (printed p. 260), degree-zero identification and middle exactness

proof.text: For injective $M$, let $N=V^S$ as in Step 4 and take $x\in N$. Choose $d$ prime to $p$ with $\sigma^d x=x$, and put $e=\ell d$. The finite cyclic norm $N_e=1+z+\cdots+z^{e-1}$ kills $x$, since $N_e x=\ell\sum_{i<d}\sigma^i x=0$. In $B_e$ the annihilator of $1-z$ is exactly $\Lambda N_e$, by the coefficient calculation in Step 2. Thus $(1-z)B_e\to N$, $(1-z)b\mapsto bx$, is a well-defined equivariant linear map. Both its domain and $B_e$ are discrete $G$-modules. Injectivity of $N$ extends it to $B_e\to N$. The image $y$ of $1$ satisfies $(1-\sigma)y=x$. Hence the last differential of $F(M)$ is surjective, and $H^2(F(M))=0$. This justifies the source's extension argument in the discrete category, without applying injectivity directly to $I\subset A$.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 1.2.2.1 (printed p. 260), last-term surjectivity in discrete modules

proof.text: The category $\operatorname{Mod}(T_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)$ is Grothendieck abelian by [lem-weil-pbc-module-sheaves-grothendieck-abelian], hence has enough injectives by [lem-sp-grothendieck-enough-injectives]. Apply [lem-sc-bounded-below-injective-resolution-existence] to choose a quasi-isomorphism $K\to J$ with $J$ bounded below and injective termwise. The ordinary derived category and supported-section functor here are exactly those in [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories] and [def-pur-etale-derived-supported-sections], so $\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,J)$ computes $R\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,K)$.

source.place: Proposition 1.2.2.1, bounded-below injective reduction; Stacks 03DA, 03DB, 03EW; Mathlib bounded-below injective replacements

proof.text: Exactness in Step 3 shows that applying each of the three degree functors of $F$ to an acyclic complex gives an acyclic complex. Filter its total complex by horizontal degree $i\ge r$ for $r=0,1,2,3$. The three successive quotients are those acyclic column complexes shifted by $i$, so the total is acyclic by the long exact sequences of these three finite filtration quotients. Apply this to the cone of $K\to J$ to obtain $F(K)\simeq F(J)$. Steps 5–6 say that each augmented row $\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,J^q)\to F(J^q)$ is a quasi-isomorphism. The cone of the total augmentation is acyclic: for a total cocycle start at its least vertical degree, solve its horizontal boundary using exactness of that augmented row, and subtract the resulting total boundary. Repeat in increasing vertical degree. At fixed total degree there are only finitely many components, because the horizontal degrees lie between $-1$ and $2$, so the process terminates. This proves $\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,J)\simeq F(J)$. The augmentation is natural and all quasi-isomorphisms can be inverted in the derived category. Therefore $F(K)$ naturally represents supported cohomology.

source.place: Proposition 1.2.2.1 (printed p. 260), totalization of the bounded-width complex and injective reduction

proof.text: Because $G$ is procyclic, its projection to $\mu_\ell(\kappa(\bar\eta))$ has kernel $\ell G$: using any generator this is the quotient of $\widehat{\mathbf Z}^{(p')}$ modulo $\ell$. Every continuous additive map from $G$ to an $\mathbf F_\ell$-vector space $N$ kills $\ell G$, and every additive map on this finite quotient is continuous and $\mathbf F_\ell$-linear. Thus $N(-1)=\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(\mu_\ell,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(G,N)$ canonically, with no action or equivariance imposed on this Hom. For $N=V$, send $f$ to the unique $A$-linear map $b:I\to V^S$ satisfying $b(1-\sigma)=\operatorname{av}_S(f(\sigma))$. Steps 2–3 give existence, uniqueness and naturality. Place this map in degree two of $F(M)$, or degree zero of $F(M)[2]$. Its target has no outgoing differential, and the source is concentrated in degree zero, so it is a cochain map $s_\sigma$. This uses the same $V$ throughout, with its actual $H$-action; no unrelated $S$-module or coefficient ring occurs.

source.place: 1.2.3 preceding Definition 1.2.3.1 (printed p. 260), twist, projector and evaluation

proof.text: We make the source's reduction for natural homotopies explicit. A homotopy from $V(-1)[0]$ to $F(M)[2]$ has just one possibly nonzero component $V(-1)\to V^S$ (degree $-1$ of $F(M)[2]$). The natural map $(0,V,0)\to(W,V,a)$ is the identity on both its source and this target, so naturality determines that component from sheaves with closed stalk zero. Next $\operatorname{av}_S:V\to V^S$ and the inclusion $V^S\to V$ are $H$-maps and are inverse on invariants. Naturality with respect to the projector forces every such component to be its value on $V^S$ preceded by $\operatorname{av}_S(-1)$. Conversely any natural component on discrete $G$-modules extends this way, and the homotopy equation extends since the two residue maps factor by the same projector. Hence existence and uniqueness reduce to $(0,N,0)$ for discrete $G$-modules $N$.

source.place: Lemma 1.2.3.2, first paragraph (printed p. 261), reduction of the natural homotopy

proof.text: Natural $\Lambda$-linear endomorphisms of the underlying-module functor on discrete $G$-modules are exactly elements of $A$. Indeed, for an open subgroup $U$, let $a_U$ be the value of the transformation on $1\in\Lambda[G/U]$. Naturality with the quotient maps makes the $a_U$ compatible. If $U$ fixes $x\in N$, the equivariant map $\Lambda[G/U]\to N$ sending $1$ to $x$ shows that the transformation sends $x$ to $a_Ux$. Conversely a compatible family acts by this formula, independent of $U$, and defines a natural endomorphism. This is also an identification of rings, by evaluating sums and compositions on $1$. In particular the natural homotopy component after the reduction in Step 10 must be multiplication by a unique $h\in A$, once evaluation at $\sigma$ identifies $N(-1)$ with $N$.

source.place: Definition 1.2.1.1 (printed pp. 259–260) and Lemma 1.2.3.2 (printed pp. 261–262), natural operations

proof.text: Evaluate $\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,N)$ at $1-\sigma$ to identify $F((0,N,0))$ with $[N\xrightarrow{1-\sigma}N]$ in degrees $1,2$. Write $\sigma'=\sigma^\alpha$ with $\alpha\in(\widehat{\mathbf Z}^{(p')})^\times$, and write $\bar\alpha\in\mathbf F_\ell^\times$ for its reduction. Since both $1-\sigma$ and $1-\sigma'$ freely generate $I$, there is a unique unit $u\in A^\times$ with $1-\sigma'=u(1-\sigma)$. In the source coordinate $x=f(\sigma)$, $f(\sigma')=\bar\alpha x$. If $b=s_{\sigma'}(f)$ then $u\,b(1-\sigma)=b(1-\sigma')=\bar\alpha x$. Thus the two cochain maps become multiplication by $1$ and by $g=\bar\alpha u^{-1}$, respectively. By Step 11 their natural homotopy is precisely a solution of $(1-\sigma)h=1-g$ in $A$.

source.place: Lemma 1.2.3.2, the complexes F_sigma, comparison maps and relation ug=alpha (printed pp. 261–262)

proof.text: For a positive integer $b$, put $v_b=\sum_{i=0}^{b-1}\sigma^i$, so $(1-\sigma)v_b=1-\sigma^b$. In the quotient $B_d$, $v_b$ depends only on $b$ modulo $\ell d$, since a sum of $\ell d$ successive powers is $\ell N_d=0$. These finite formulas therefore extend continuously and compatibly to $b\in\widehat{\mathbf Z}^{(p')}$, giving $v_b\in A$ with $\epsilon(v_b)=b\bmod\ell$. At $b=\alpha$ injectivity in Step 2 gives $v_\alpha=u$. Hence $\epsilon(u)=\bar\alpha$, and $\epsilon(g)=\bar\alpha/\epsilon(u)=1$. Thus $1-g\in I$. Step 2 now provides the unique $h\in A$ with $(1-\sigma)h=1-g$. Steps 10–12 turn it into the unique homotopy natural in all sheaves $M$, proving the exact generator-independence assertion. The uniqueness concerns natural homotopies, not homotopies for one isolated module.

Apply $s_\sigma$ termwise to $K$ and totalize, using total differential $d_F+(-1)^i d_K$ in horizontal degree $i$. This gives $K_{\bar\eta}(-1)\to F(K)[2]$. Naturality of the degree-$-1$ homotopy components in Step 13 makes them commute with $d_K$; their horizontal degree drops by one, so the two vertical terms in the total homotopy equation have opposite signs and cancel. Thus generator changes give homotopic total maps. Each degree of this totalization has only three summands. Since $F$ and the stalk/twist functors preserve quasi-isomorphisms, these natural maps descend to the localization defining $D^+$. The one-dimensional vector space $L=\mu_\ell(\kappa(\bar\eta))$ satisfies $\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(L,N)\otimes_\Lambda L\cong N$ by evaluation. Tensor the map with $L$ and use Step 8 to obtain $\operatorname{sp}_T:K_{\bar\eta}\to R\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,K)(1)[2]$, natural in $K$ and independent of the representative and generator.
